transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop thinking about my face. The left side of it, specifically. To me, it looks really crooked and just messed up. 

It's basically all I think about. When I'm working at the warehouse, or even if I try to go out to salsa night, I just feel like everyone is staring at it and noticing how uneven it is. People tell me they don't see anything wrong when I bring it up, but... I know it's there. I just can't get past it, and it's really getting to me.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time repeatedly checking your face in mirrors or other reflective surfaces?

Yeah, I do. It happens a lot at work, actually. Before I go back out on the inventory floor, I'll stop in the bathroom and just keep checking my face in the mirror. 

I end up fixing my cap over and over to try and hide it, and rubbing at that same spot on the left side. I get stuck doing it, and sometimes I'm in there for so long that I'm late getting back. My picking numbers end up falling behind, and my boss keeps getting on me about it. But I just can't seem to stop checking.
Deep down, do you ever feel that your face might actually look normal and your mind is exaggerating it, or are you completely certain it is deformed?

I'm not really sure. I mean... people tell me they don't see anything, so I hear what they're saying. But when I actually look in the mirror, I'm certain it's crooked. I just see what I see. I don't really know if my mind is exaggerating it or not, because to me, it just looks completely messed up.

latest_inference.note: Patient demonstrates poor to fair insight ('I don't really know if my mind is exaggerating it or not') rather than a completely fixed unshakeable delusion, ruling out delusional disorder (F22) and confirming body dysmorphic disorder under F45.2.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits persistent preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance (perceived asymmetry of the face) that is not visible to others. This preoccupation leads to repetitive behaviors including excessive mirror checking, camouflaging with a cap, and touching the area, causing noticeable occupational impairment. Under ICD-10, body dysmorphic disorder is classified under F45.2 (Hypochondriacal disorder).

confirmed_symptoms: Preoccupation with perceived crookedness/defect on the left side of the face
Belief that others notice and stare at the perceived defect despite reassurance that nothing is wrong
Repetitive mirror checking in the bathroom
Repetitive camouflaging behaviors (fixing cap to hide face, rubbing the area)

additional_requirements: Perceived defect is not observable or appears negligible to others
Repeated mirror checking and grooming causing work delays and decreased performance
